lessons.title: Planting Techniques: Hole Preparation and Spacing
lessons.body: Planting holes for bananas should be dug at least 60 cm wide and 60 cm deep. In dry areas, make them 80 cm deep to reach moist soil. Separate topsoil (first 30 cm) from subsoil. Mix topsoil with 1 bucket (about 10 kg) of well-rotted manure or compost and 100 g of triple superphosphate (TSP). If you don't have TSP, use 200 g of wood ash. This mixture goes back into the hole first. Spacing depends on variety and purpose. For dessert bananas (like Cavendish), use 2.5 m between plants and 3 m between rows (about 1,300 plants per hectare). For cooking bananas (like Matooke), use 3 m by 3 m (about 1,100 plants per hectare). In windy areas, plant closer (2 m by 2.5 m) for mutual support. Dig holes at least 2 weeks before planting to let soil settle and sun sterilize pests. On slopes, dig holes with the back edge higher to catch water. Plant the sucker so the corm (the round base) is 5 cm below soil level. Fill the hole halfway, firm the soil, then fill to the top. Do not bury the pseudostem (the trunk-like part). Water immediately with 10-20 liters per plant. If using tissue-culture plantlets, handle gently and plant at the same depth they were in the nursery. Always plant on a day when rain is expected or in the late afternoon to reduce shock.

lessons.title: Optimal Planting Seasons and Timing
lessons.body: In Africa, the best time to plant bananas is at the start of the rainy season. For most of West Africa, this is April to June. In East Africa (Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania), plant in March to May or September to November. In Southern Africa, plant in October to December. The goal is to give young plants 3-4 months of regular rain before a dry spell. If you have irrigation, you can plant any time except during heavy rains that cause waterlogging. Avoid planting in the middle of a dry season unless you can water every 2-3 days. Also avoid planting right before a known dry spell. For example, in Nigeria, do not plant in July if you know August will be dry (August break). Plant suckers that are 30-50 cm tall with at least 3 healthy leaves. Smaller suckers take longer to establish. If you must plant in a dry month, dig the hole, fill it with water, let it drain, then plant, and mulch heavily. In flood-prone areas, plant on raised beds or ridges 30 cm high. Timing also affects harvest. Bananas take 9-12 months from planting to harvest. So if you plant in April, you harvest the following January to March. That may be a good market time. Check local prices: often bananas are scarce in the dry season, so planting to harvest then can bring higher prices. Always keep a planting calendar and record the date you plant each block.

lessons.title: Mulching and Weed Control
lessons.body: Mulching is covering the soil around banana plants with dry organic material. It conserves moisture, suppresses weeds, and adds nutrients as it rots. Use dry grass, banana leaves, maize stover, or coffee husks. Spread a layer 5-10 cm thick, but keep it 15 cm away from the pseudostem to prevent rot. Do not use fresh grass or materials that may carry pests. Reapply mulch every 3-4 months. Weeds compete for water and nutrients. The worst weeds in banana fields are couch grass, spear grass, and black jack. Control them early. Hand-hoe or slash weeds before they flower. Do not dig deep near banana rootsâthey are shallow (top 30 cm). Shallow weeding with a hoe is best. For large farms, use a slasher or string trimmer. Herbicides like glyphosate can be used but must be applied carefully to avoid contact with banana leaves. Spray only on a calm day and use a shield. Mulching alone reduces weed growth by 70-80%. If you mulch heavily, you may only need to weed 2-3 times per year instead of 6-8. In dry areas, mulch is critical to keep soil moist. In wet areas, mulch prevents soil erosion. Combine mulch with cover crops like beans or groundnuts between rows. These fix nitrogen and provide extra income. Never let weeds go to seedâone weed can produce thousands of seeds. Keep a clean field for the first 6 months, and the banana plants will shade out many weeds later.

lessons.title: Irrigation Systems for Young Plants
lessons.body: Young banana plants need 25-50 mm of water per week. If rainfall is less than this, you must irrigate. The simplest method is a watering can: give each plant 10-20 liters every 2-3 days for the first 2 months. For larger areas, use drip irrigation. A drip line with emitters every 30 cm can water a row of bananas. Drip saves water and reduces weeds. Install one drip line per row, 30 cm from the plant base. Run it for 1-2 hours every day or every other day. You can also use furrow irrigation: make small channels between rows and let water flow. But furrows can spread diseases and erode soil. For small plots, use a hose with a nozzle. Check soil moisture by digging 10 cm deepâif dry, water. Overwatering causes root rot. In waterlogged soils, make raised beds. Catch and store rainwater in tanks or ponds. A 5,000-liter tank can irrigate 100 young plants for 2 weeks. Solar-powered pumps are becoming affordable in Africa. In dry months, water in the early morning or late evening to reduce evaporation. Mulch heavily to keep moisture. If leaves roll up or turn yellow, the plant is stressedâwater immediately. After 6 months, banana roots go deeper and need less frequent watering, but still need 25 mm per week. Always monitor your plants daily for the first month after planting.

lessons.title: Fertilization at Planting and Early Growth
lessons.body: At planting, mix 100 g of TSP (triple superphosphate) or 200 g of bone meal into the topsoil that goes back into the hole. This helps root development. Do not use nitrogen fertilizers at plantingâthey can burn young roots. Four weeks after planting, apply 50 g of urea or 100 g of NPK 17-17-17 per plant. Spread it in a ring 20 cm from the pseudostem, then cover with soil. Repeat every 2 months for the first year. For organic farmers, use 5 kg of well-rotted manure or compost per plant every 3 months. You can also use kitchen ash (wood ash) at 200 g per plantâit provides potassium. Banana plants need a lot of potassium (K) for fruit filling. A mature plant removes 200 g of K from the soil per year. So after 6 months, switch to a fertilizer high in potassium, like NPK 12-12-17 or 0-0-60 (muriate of potash). Apply 100 g per plant every 2 months. In sandy soils, apply smaller amounts more often. In clay soils, less frequent. Always water after applying fertilizer. Do not apply fertilizer to dry soilâit can damage roots. Foliar sprays of zinc or boron can correct deficiencies if leaves show stripes or deformities. Keep a record of what you apply and when. Over-fertilizing with nitrogen causes lots of leaves but no fruit. Under-fertilizing causes small bunches. Test your soil every 2 years if possible.

lessons.title: Gap Filling and Replanting
lessons.body: Even with good care, some plants die or fail to grow. You must replace them to keep your field full and productive. Check your field every week for the first 3 months. A plant is dead if the pseudostem is rotten or the leaves are completely dry. To replant, dig out the dead plant and its corm. Do not leave old rootsâthey may harbor pests. Dig a new hole 60 cm wide and deep, and mix in compost and a little TSP. Plant a healthy sucker of the same variety. If the gap is due to disease (like Panama wilt), do not replant banana there for at least 2 years. Instead, plant a cover crop like beans or maize. For gaps caused by wind or animals, replant immediately. The best time to gap-fill is early in the rainy season so the new plant catches up. If you plant a sucker that is 30-50 cm tall, it will be only 2-3 months behind the original plants. If you wait too long, the gap reduces your yield. A 10% gap means 10% less harvest. Also, gaps allow weeds to grow. After replanting, water the new sucker and mulch it. Keep a nursery of extra suckers near your fieldâplant 5% more than you need. That way you always have replacement material. If a plant is weak but not dead, you can nurse it with extra water and fertilizer. But if it is stunted after 2 months, replace it. Record the date of replanting so you can manage it separately.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Planting and Early Field Management of Bananas in Africa

This module covers the field operations that determine whether a banana plantation becomes a profitable enterprise or an expensive lesson. Banana farming in Africa rewards precision at planting and disciplined early management. The first 90 days after planting set the yield ceiling for the entire cycle. Get hole preparation, timing, mulching, irrigation, fertilization and gap filling right, and you protect your investment. Get them wrong, and you spend the rest of the cycle compensating for problems that were avoidable.

This reference is written for commercial and semi-commercial growers across sub-Saharan Africa, from the highlands of Uganda and Rwanda to the lowland zones of Ghana, Nigeria, Kenya and Tanzania. It assumes you are growing for market, not subsistence, and that every input decision must return more than it costs.

Planting Techniques: Hole Preparation and Spacing

Banana is a heavy feeder with a shallow, brittle root system. Hole preparation is not about digging a hole; it is about creating a rooting environment that supports 20â40 tonnes per hectare of marketable fruit. In most African soils, the limiting factors are compaction, low organic matter and poor drainage.

Prepare holes at least 60 cm Ã 60 cm Ã 60 cm for tissue-culture plantlets and 45 cm Ã 45 cm Ã 45 cm for healthy suckers. In heavy clay or lateritic soils, widen to 60â80 cm and break the subsoil base to improve drainage. Separate topsoil from subsoil and return topsoil first, mixed with 10â20 kg of well-decomposed manure or compost per hole. This single practice can increase early pseudostem circumference by 15â25%, which directly correlates with bunch weight.

Spacing depends on cultivar, market and mechanization. For dessert bananas (Cavendish types) in commercial blocks, 2.5 m Ã 2.5 m (1,600 plants/ha) to 3 m Ã 2 m (1,667 plants/ha) is standard. For plantains and East African highland cooking bananas (AAA-EA), 3 m Ã 3 m (1,111 plants/ha) is common in Uganda and Rwanda. Wider spacing improves airflow and reduces Sigatoka pressure; tighter spacing raises early yield per hectare but increases disease risk and labor for deleafing.

Optimal Planting Seasons and Timing

Timing is a financial decision. Planting at the start of the rainy season lets the plant establish before dry stress, reduces irrigation cost and brings the first harvest into a favorable market window 9â12 months later. In Uganda's Lake Victoria crescent, the two main planting windows are MarchâMay and SeptemberâNovember. In Kenya's central highlands, MarchâApril and OctoberâNovember. In Ghana and Nigeria's forest zones, the major season (AprilâJune) is preferred over the minor season (SeptemberâOctober) because early root development is stronger.

Avoid planting in the middle of a heavy rainy peak on poorly drained soils; waterlogging in the first two weeks causes root rot and high mortality. If you must plant in the dry season, budget for irrigation from day one and use mulch immediately.

Mulching and Weed Control

Mulch is the cheapest yield-boosting input in African banana farming. A 10â15 cm layer of dry grass, banana pseudostem chop, coffee husk or maize stover around the mat conserves soil moisture, suppresses weeds, moderates soil temperature and adds organic matter. Keep mulch 15â20 cm away from the pseudostem to avoid collar rot and rodent damage.

Weed control in the first six months must be rigorous. Bananas are poor competitors. Hand-weed or use selective herbicides; never use glyphosate near young suckers or exposed roots. A clean, mulched plantation can reduce weeding labor by 40â60% compared to bare-soil systems.

Irrigation Systems for Young Plants

Young banana plants need 25â35 mm of water per week. In rain-fed systems, mulch and planting timing handle most of this. In dry zones or for high-density commercial blocks, drip irrigation is the most water-efficient and fertilizer-compatible option. Drip at 2â4 L/hour per plant, two emitters per mat, delivers water directly to the root zone and cuts evaporation losses by 30â50% compared to overhead sprinkler.

Overhead sprinklers are cheaper to install but increase leaf wetness and Sigatoka risk. Furrow irrigation works in flat, well-drained soils but wastes water and spreads weeds. For most African commercial growers, a hybrid approach works: drip for establishment, mulch to buffer dry spells.

Fertilization at Planting and Early Growth

Banana removes roughly 200 kg N, 50 kg PâOâ and 400 kg KâO per hectare per year at commercial yields. Early fertilization builds the pseudostem that will carry the bunch. At planting, mix 10â20 kg manure or compost plus 100â150 g of triple superphosphate (TSP) or rock phosphate per hole. From one month after planting, apply 50â100 g of NPK 17-17-17 or a similar balanced blend per plant per month, split into two applications during the rainy season.

From month three, shift toward potassium: muriate of potash (MOP, 0-0-60) at 100â150 g per plant per month improves bunch size and fruit filling. Always apply fertilizer in a ring 20â30 cm from the pseudostem, not against the base, and water it in.

Table 1: Recommended Early Fertilization Schedule (per plant)

Stage Product Rate Frequency Notes
At planting Manure/compost + TSP 10â20 kg + 100â150 g Once Mix into backfill soil
Month 1â2 NPK 17-17-17 50â80 g Monthly Ring application, water in
Month 3â4 NPK 17-17-17 80â100 g Monthly Split during rains
Month 5â6 MOP (0-0-60) 100â150 g Monthly Builds bunch potential
Month 7+ MOP + urea (top-dress) 150 g + 50 g Every 6â8 weeks Adjust to leaf analysis

Source: Adapted from NARO Uganda banana agronomy recommendations (2021) and IITA Banana and Plantain Fertilizer Guidelines (2022).

Gap Filling and Replanting

Plant mortality in the first three months should not exceed 5%. Walk the field weekly. Replace dead or severely stunted plants with healthy suckers or tissue-culture plantlets of the same cultivar and age class. Gap filling must happen within 4â6 weeks of planting; later replacements create uneven stands, complicate harvesting and reduce block uniformity.

Use only certified disease-free planting material. In East Africa, tissue-culture plantlets from accredited labs (e.g., NARO, KALRO, IITA) reduce pest and disease risk and give 20â30% higher yields than sucker-derived plants. For suckers, select sword suckers 30â50 cm tall with healthy corms.

Table 2: Planting Material Options and Business Trade-offs

Material Cost Establishment Disease Risk Yield Potential Best For
Tissue-culture plantlet High (USD 0.50â1.50/plant) Slow first 4 weeks, then vigorous Low High (30â40 t/ha) Commercial blocks, export
Sword sucker Low (USD 0.05â0.20) Fast MediumâHigh Medium (15â25 t/ha) Smallholders, local market
Macropropagated plantlet Medium (USD 0.30â0.80) Moderate LowâMedium High (25â35 t/ha) Mid-scale commercial

Source: IITA Banana Seed Systems in Sub-Saharan Africa (2022); NARO Uganda tissue-culture cost data (2021).

â  SAFETY WARNING â PESTICIDE AND FERTILIZER HANDLING

Always wear gloves, boots, long sleeves and eye protection when handling fertilizers, herbicides or nematicides. Never apply glyphosate or other systemic herbicides to young banana suckers or exposed roots â this causes pseudostem distortion and plant death. Store all agrochemicals in a locked, ventilated area away from food, water sources and children. Wash hands and equipment after every application. In case of skin or eye contact, rinse with clean water for 15 minutes and seek medical attention.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Prepare holes 60 Ã 60 Ã 60 cm (45 cm for suckers), separate topsoil, mix 10â20 kg manure + 100â150 g TSP into backfill.
  • Plant at the start of the rainy season (MarchâMay or SeptâNov in East Africa) to cut irrigation cost and reduce mortality.
  • Space at 2.5 Ã 2.5 m for dessert bananas (1,600/ha) or 3 Ã 3 m for plantains/highland cooking types (1,111/ha).
  • Mulch immediately with 10â15 cm of dry grass or crop residue, keeping 15â20 cm clear of the pseudostem.
  • Weed rigorously for the first 6 months â hand-weed or use selective herbicides; never glyphosate near young plants.
  • Irrigate 25â35 mm/week; drip at 2â4 L/hour per plant is the most efficient for dry zones.
  • Fertilize monthly from month 1 with NPK 17-17-17, shifting to MOP from month 3â5 for bunch development.
  • Gap-fill within 4â6 weeks using certified disease-free tissue-culture plantlets or healthy sword suckers of the same cultivar.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Banana and Plantain Programme (free technical resources and country data)
  • IITA â Banana and Plantain Research and Production Guides
  • NARO Uganda â National Banana Research Programme (agronomy, tissue culture, pest management)
  • KALRO Kenya â Banana Production and Value Chain Resources
  • Bioversity International â Banana Genetic Resources and Sustainable Production

This module is part of the Rise AFRICA Skills â Banana Farming course. All figures are indicative for sub-Saharan African conditions; validate locally with your extension officer or agronomist before large-scale adoption.

quiz.q: What is the recommended size for a banana planting hole?
options: A) 30 cm wide and 30 cm deep
B) 60 cm wide and 60 cm deep
C) 100 cm wide and 100 cm deep
D) 40 cm wide and 20 cm deep
quiz.explanation: A 60 cm by 60 cm hole allows proper root development and space for compost.

quiz.q: Which material should be mixed with topsoil when planting bananas?
quiz.explanation: Well-rotted manure and TSP provide nutrients without burning roots.

quiz.q: What is the correct spacing for dessert bananas like Cavendish?
quiz.explanation: 2.5 m by 3 m gives about 1,300 plants per hectare, ideal for dessert bananas.

quiz.q: How deep should the corm be planted below soil level?
quiz.explanation: Planting the corm 5 cm below soil level protects it but keeps the pseudostem above ground.

quiz.q: Why should you dig holes at least 2 weeks before planting?
options: A) To let the soil dry out completely
B) To allow soil to settle and sun sterilize pests
C) To encourage weeds to grow
D) To make the hole deeper
quiz.explanation: Sun exposure helps kill soil pests and the soil settles, preventing air pockets.

quiz.q: In West Africa, what is the best planting time for bananas?
quiz.explanation: April to June is the start of the rainy season, giving young plants moisture.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid planting bananas in the middle of a dry season?
options: A) The soil is too fertile
B) Young plants need regular water and will die
C) Bananas grow faster in dry heat
quiz.explanation: Without irrigation, dry season planting leads to water stress and death.

quiz.q: How long does it take from planting to harvest for bananas?
quiz.explanation: Bananas typically take 9-12 months from planting to harvest.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of planting on raised beds in flood-prone areas?
quiz.explanation: Raised beds keep roots above waterlogged soil, preventing rot.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of mulching banana plants?
options: B) To conserve moisture and suppress weeds
D) To provide shade for leaves
quiz.explanation: Mulch reduces evaporation and blocks weed growth.

quiz.q: How thick should a mulch layer be?
quiz.explanation: A 5-10 cm layer is enough to conserve moisture without smothering the plant.

quiz.q: Why should mulch be kept 15 cm away from the pseudostem?
options: A) To allow air and prevent rot
quiz.explanation: Keeping mulch away prevents excessive moisture that can cause stem rot.

quiz.q: Which weed is mentioned as a major problem in banana fields?
quiz.explanation: Couch grass is a common aggressive weed that competes with bananas.

quiz.q: What is the best way to control weeds in a banana field?
options: B) Shallow weeding with a hoe
quiz.explanation: Banana roots are shallow, so deep digging damages them.

quiz.q: How much water does a young banana plant need per week?
quiz.explanation: 25-50 mm per week is the recommended amount for young plants.

quiz.q: Which irrigation method is most water-efficient for bananas?
quiz.explanation: Drip irrigation delivers water directly to roots with minimal loss.

quiz.q: When is the best time to water banana plants?
options: B) Early morning or late evening
quiz.explanation: Watering in cooler parts of the day reduces evaporation losses.

quiz.q: What sign indicates a banana plant needs water?
options: A) Leaves roll up or turn yellow
quiz.explanation: Rolled or yellow leaves are signs of water stress.

quiz.q: What fertilizer is recommended at planting for root development?
quiz.explanation: TSP or bone meal provides phosphorus for strong root growth.

quiz.q: When should you first apply nitrogen fertilizer after planting?
quiz.explanation: Applying nitrogen too early can burn roots; wait 4 weeks.

quiz.q: How much urea is recommended per plant at first application?
quiz.explanation: 50 g of urea per plant is a safe initial dose.

quiz.q: Which nutrient do banana plants need most for fruit filling?
quiz.explanation: Potassium is critical for bunch size and fruit quality.

quiz.q: What is a good organic source of potassium for bananas?
quiz.explanation: Wood ash is rich in potassium and can be used as a fertilizer.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid applying fertilizer to dry soil?
options: B) It makes the soil too wet
quiz.explanation: Fertilizer on dry soil can burn plant roots due to high salt concentration.

quiz.q: How often should you check for gaps in a newly planted banana field?
options: B) Every week for the first 3 months
quiz.explanation: Weekly checks allow early replacement of dead plants.

quiz.q: What should you do with the old corm when replanting a gap?
options: A) Leave it in the hole
D) Cut it and leave it
quiz.explanation: Old corms can harbor pests and diseases, so remove them.

quiz.q: If a plant dies from Panama wilt, when can you replant banana there?
quiz.explanation: Panama wilt persists in soil, so a 2-year break with other crops is needed.

quiz.q: What is a good practice to ensure you have replacement suckers?
options: B) Keep a nursery of extra suckers
quiz.explanation: A nursery with 5% extra suckers ensures you can fill gaps quickly.

quiz.q: How much yield can be lost if 10% of plants are missing?
quiz.explanation: Each missing plant reduces total harvest proportionally.

quiz.q: What should you do if a weak plant is still stunted after 2 months?
quiz.explanation: Stunted plants rarely catch up and are better replaced.
